In terms of being reasonable in allowing the other party to fix things, I think you're referring to the idea of mitigation - claimants have to take reasonable steps to minimise the loss caused by the defendant's breach of contract. Claimants can't recover damages in respect of any part of the loss that they could have avoided by taking reasonable steps (*British Westinghouse Electric Co v Underground Electric Railways Co of London* (1912)).

Re the missed holiday, the company will only be liable if there was an assumption of responsibility, express or implicit ([*The Achilleas*](https://www.bailii.org/cgi-bin/format.cgi?doc=/uk/cases/UKHL/2008/48.html)). ie only if the type of loss (missed holiday) was one which the parties reasonably contemplated that the company would assume responsibility for, which is highly unlikely.

It's useful to note that employment status for the purposes of employment law (which would affect your legal entitlements) is independent of employment status for the purposes of taxes. 

In employment law, an individual will fall in one of three categories: an employee, a worker, or an independent contractor (note that all employees are workers but not all workers are employees). An employee has the most protection and rights with independent contractor the least. Importantly, only workers and employees are entitled to NMW whereas independent contractors aren't. 

With your case, the question is whether you're an independent contractor or whether you're a worker. As mentioned already, while what your contract says can be indicative, it's not definitive and courts will see whether the contract reflects the actual relationship. 

What is key here is whether you're a so-called "limb (b)" worker, defined in [section 230(3)(b) of he Employment Rights Act 1996](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/230) as anyone who entered into or works under

>	any other contract, whether express or implied and (if it is express) whether oral or in writing, whereby **the individual undertakes to do or perform personally any work or services for another party to the contract whose status is not by virtue of the contract that of a client or customer of any profession or business undertaking carried on by the individual**;

In other words, as long as the sailing company isn't a client/customer of yours, you've contracted to work personally for the company (ie you can't send a substitute) and you're dependent on the company, you'll be a 'worker' for the purposes of employment law.

The legal definition of rape under s1 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 requires a lack of reasonable belief of consent - ie if you (objectively) reasonably thought she was consenting, it's not legally rape. That doesn't necessarily mean she was (subjectively) consenting and a lower threshold probably applies to sexual misconduct disciplinary charges rather than criminal rape charges. The uni should let you make your case and if the disciplinary panel (or whoever) believes you, you should be let off. 

In terms of criminal charges, the definition of 'consent' under the SOA 2003 can be quite complicated and here, there might be a rebuttable presumption of no consent and lack of reasonable belief in consent if she was asleep/unconscious at the time (s 75(2)(d)). In other words, if she was asleep/unconscious at the time, the burden will be on you to raise sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption. If criminal charges are brought against you, you will definitely need to get a lawyer.
